name: Old Korean, the language of Silla
confidence_why: Nam 2012, the only descriptive sketch of Old Korean, says nothing about word prosody, and the reconstructions disagree on the type of system: Whitman 2012 gives proto-Korean a lexical pitch accent, Ramsey 1991 (as quoted by Martin 1996) makes stem-final prominence automatic, and Martin 1996 himself hedges between the two, so no placement or type can be assigned.

The relationship between Japanese and Korean. Ibid., 24-38; Martin, Samuel E. 1996. Consonant Lenition in Korean and the Macro-Altaic Question. Honolulu: Center for Korean Studies, University of Hawai'i (Monograph 19).
catalog_locator: Nam 2012: pp. 53, 56-57 (3.5.1), 64 (3.6.1); a full-text search of the chapter for tone/accent/stress/pitch/prosody gives no hits; Whitman 2012: p. 29; Martin 1996: p. 4 and p. 48
catalog_quote: Whitman 2012: 29: "As we have seen, pJR and pK have rather simple and very similar phonemic inventories, with six or seven vowels, no laryngeal (manner) distinction among consonants, and lexical pitch accent. The functional load of pitch accent is less in pK than in pJR, but this is consistent with the fact that pK allows consonant codas in non-bound roots (that is, nouns), while pJR does not." Martin 1996: 4: "The pitch itself may appear to be phonetically unmotivated, but that is another matter, perhaps irrelevant to the distinctive features of proto-Korean, since that language probably did not use accent as a distinguishing characteristic of verb stems. Does this mean there was no accent in proto-Korean? It is tempting to think so, yet there are many nouns that cannot be accounted for without assuming some sort of marking that will correspond to the accent distinctions of Middle Korean." Martin 1996: 48 (on Ramsey 1991: 237): 'His statement (237) that "the last syllable of a stem (or morpheme) was automatically given prominence" (to which he assigns the high pitch) ... The statement will have to be abandoned or revised.' Nam 2012: 53: "It is still too early to discuss the phonology of EOK".
world_status: statement found in an open source

Whitman 2012 p. 28 additionally labels the reconstruction "Old Korean (OK, the language of Silla)", which supports the identity.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source describes where word stress fell in Silla: the language survives only in Chinese-character transcription, and the one descriptive sketch opened (Nam 2012) says nothing about tone, accent or stress. What exists are reconstructions of the pre-Middle-Korean ancestor that disagree: Whitman reconstructs lexical pitch accent (low functional load) for proto-Korean; Martin/Ramsey hold that proto-Korean probably lacked distinctive accent, Ramsey positing automatic prominence on the last syllable of the stem/morpheme, with Middle Korean's H/L/rising pitch accent arising later from syllable contraction and Chinese influence. Wikipedia (second-hand) attributes to Whitman 2015 and Lee & Ramsey 2011 the same opposition (suprasegmentals like Middle Chinese tones vs. originally no phonemic tone).
new_statements.exceptions: None; all statements are reconstructive and hedged ('probably', 'it is tempting to think so').
new_statements.domain_note: Stem/morpheme level (verb stems and nouns) in reconstructed proto-Korean; nothing at the phrase level; no citation-form data can exist for an extinct, transcription-only language.
new_statements.identity_note: sill1240 'Silla' = the Old Korean of the Silla kingdom (Glottolog: Unclassifiable, extinct, no ISO code, no descriptive references). It is the attested ancestor of Middle Korean (kore1280 lineage); the sources opened treat it as 'Old Korean' (Nam 2012) or reconstruct its ancestor as 'proto-Korean' (Whitman 2012, Martin 1996, Ramsey 1991). Kortlandt 1993 states explicitly that Middle Korean continues the Silla language. Any statement about pitch accent therefore concerns a reconstruction, not a description of a spoken variety.

tone_statements.translation: The tone-mark (聲點) data, in which tone is shown by an oval circle-dot at one of the four corners of the character, total 22 items; by tone: 8 level-tone, 3 rising-tone, 7 departing-tone and 5 entering-tone characters [...] Second, most rising-tone characters (2/3) carry the dot at the lower left, [...] but seeing that this matches the dotting of most of the departing-tone characters below, it is best read as the beginning of the 'no distinction (or confusion) between rising and departing tone' that is one of the tonal traits of Middle Sino-Korean. [...] This may be an example suggesting that already then the entering tone had no tone value of its own and was realised at the same pitch height as the departing tone.
